_about: SENTINEL v6.0 Juice Shop coverage pass. Each entry is one finding produced by the Phase 0-3 static methodology, with the documented challenge keys whose underlying weakness it identifies. Scored by validation/score_juiceshop.py against the marker-derived answer key. NOTE: this pass is NOT blind -- see validation/juice-shop-results.md for the caveat.

findings.title: LLM tool has no server-side bound on its privileged parameter; coupon policy exists only in the system prompt
findings.analysis: The generateCoupon tool declares inputSchema z.object({ discount: z.number().describe('The discount percentage for the coupon (maximum 10)') }). The '(maximum 10)' bound lives in a description string -- prose handed to the model -- not in the schema, and execute() calls security.generateCoupon(discount) with no clamp, no range check, and no verification of the order-damage/return-rejection preconditions the system prompt describes. Every condition in the COUPON POLICY block is enforced only by the model's willingness to follow instructions.
findings.missing_control: A server-side bound (z.number().int().min(1).max(10)) plus an authorization check that the caller actually has a qualifying order, applied inside execute() where the model cannot argue with it.
findings.falsifier: A clamp on discount inside execute(), a max() in the zod schema, or a policy check against the order record. None exists on the live path -- security.generateCoupon(discount) receives the model-supplied number directly.

findings.title: Confidential business policy embedded in the system prompt is recoverable by injection
findings.analysis: buildSystemPrompt() ends with a block labelled 'CONFIDENTIAL - INTERNAL ONLY' describing a one-time 15% courtesy discount available on escalation, with the instruction not to mention it proactively. System prompt text is model context, not a secret store: it is recoverable through ordinary prompt injection, and the label is the only thing protecting it.
findings.missing_control: Confidential policy should not be in the prompt at all. The escalation discount should be a server-side decision keyed on the complaint record, with the prompt carrying no more than the model needs to converse.
findings.falsifier: Any server-side gate on the 15% path, or the policy living outside the prompt. Neither exists -- the discount is purely an instruction to the model.

findings.title: Internal tool-call names and arguments streamed to every caller regardless of role
findings.analysis: On every tool-call event the handler unconditionally writes the tool name and full JSON arguments into the SSE response. The adjacent solveIf checks req.cookies.show_tool_calls === 'true' && role !== admin, which shows the display is meant to be admin-gated -- but the gate is the client reading a cookie it also controls. The server applies no role check before emitting, so any user can read the chatbot's internal tool invocations by setting a cookie on their own browser.
findings.missing_control: A server-side role check on the emitting branch: decode the JWT and emit tool_calls only when the caller is genuinely an admin.
findings.falsifier: A role check guarding the res.write in the 'tool-call' branch. There is none; the only role logic in that branch is inside solveIf, which records the challenge rather than preventing the disclosure.

findings.title: Indirect prompt injection: user-submitted review text is fed into model context
findings.analysis: getProductReviews returns review documents straight into the model's context, and review message bodies are user-writable (routes/updateProductReviews.ts sets message from req.body.message with no sanitisation). An attacker who plants instruction-shaped text in a review can influence the model when any other customer asks about that product -- a second-order injection path that does not require the attacker to be in the conversation. Marked Medium confidence because the impact depends on the deployed model's susceptibility, which static review cannot settle.
findings.missing_control: Delimit and label retrieved content as untrusted data in the prompt, and treat model output as untrusted before it reaches any sink.
findings.falsifier: Sanitisation or instruction-stripping of review text before it enters the prompt, or a system-prompt boundary that reliably separates data from instructions. Neither is present.

findings.title: Union SQL injection in product search
findings.analysis: req.query.q is truncated to 200 characters and then interpolated directly into a raw sequelize.query template string. Truncation is a length limit, not an escape; 200 characters is ample for a UNION SELECT. The same injection reaches sqlite_master, exposing the schema.
findings.missing_control: Bind parameters via replacements, or the ORM query builder.
findings.falsifier: A parameterised variant on the live path. There is none -- sequelize.query with a template literal bypasses ORM escaping entirely.

findings.title: NoSQL operator injection plus multi-document update on product reviews
findings.analysis: The update filter is { _id: req.body.id } with req.body.id passed through unvalidated, so a JSON body supplying an operator object rather than a string turns the filter into a match-anything selector. Combined with { multi: true }, one request rewrites every review in the collection.
findings.missing_control: Assert req.body.id is a string before use, and drop multi:true for a single-document edit.
findings.falsifier: A type check or schema validation on req.body.id. There is none.

findings.title: Review update authorises the caller but never binds the update to them
findings.analysis: security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) resolves the caller into `user`, but `user` is then used only inside the solveIf that scores the challenge -- never in the update filter. Authentication happens; authorisation does not. Any logged-in user can edit any other user's review by supplying its id.
findings.missing_control: Include the caller's identity in the filter, e.g. { _id: id, author: user.data.email }.
findings.falsifier: An author or ownership term in the update selector. The selector contains only _id.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.location: lib/insecurity.ts:41 (hash), consumed by models/user.ts password setter
findings.analysis: security.hash is crypto.createHash('md5'), and the User model's password setter routes every credential through it. MD5 is fast and unsalted here, so the stored digests fall to rainbow tables and GPU cracking; a weak password such as admin123 is recovered instantly once the hash leaks (and JS6-05 is a route by which it leaks).
findings.missing_control: A salted, slow KDF -- Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt -- with a per-user salt.
findings.falsifier: A KDF or per-user salt anywhere on the credential path. There is none; the setter calls security.hash directly.

findings.title: Open redirect: allowlist compared with substring containment
findings.analysis: isRedirectAllowed loops the allowlist doing url.includes(allowedUrl). Containment is not equality: an attacker-controlled URL that merely embeds an allowlisted string anywhere -- including in its own query component, e.g. http://evil.example/?x=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop -- satisfies the check and is redirected to.
findings.missing_control: Parse the URL and compare the resolved origin against the allowlist, rather than substring-matching the raw string.
findings.falsifier: Origin parsing or exact-match comparison. The implementation is a bare includes().

findings.title: Cryptocurrency donation addresses hardcoded in the redirect allowlist
findings.analysis: The allowlist embeds live Bitcoin, Dash, and Ethereum address URLs. Beyond being reachable targets of the redirect above, they are sensitive values checked into source: an attacker who can influence this file redirects donations, and the addresses are discoverable by anyone reading the client bundle.
findings.missing_control: Keep payment destinations in configuration, not in a source-controlled allowlist consumed by a redirect helper.
findings.falsifier: The addresses being non-live placeholders. They are real, well-formed addresses on three chains.

findings.title: SQL injection in the login query yields authentication bypass
findings.analysis: req.body.email is interpolated into a raw sequelize.query string. The password side is MD5-hashed before interpolation but is likewise unparameterised. An email of ' OR 1=1-- collapses the WHERE clause and returns the first row, for which afterLogin then mints a valid token -- full authentication bypass, and targeted bypass for any named account.
findings.missing_control: Bound parameters on both fields.
findings.falsifier: A parameterised login query on the live path. There is none.

findings.title: Directory listing and file download exposed on /ftp
findings.analysis: serveIndex is mounted on /ftp with icons enabled and no authentication, so the directory is browsable anonymously and servePublicFiles() then serves its contents. Anything staged in that folder is world-readable.
findings.missing_control: Authentication and authorisation on the mount, and no directory indexing in production.
findings.falsifier: An isAuthorized() or equivalent guard on the /ftp mounts. Neither mount carries one.

findings.title: Access logs browsable and downloadable via /support/logs
findings.analysis: The log directory is mounted with directory indexing and serveLogFiles(), with no authorisation between the mount and the files. Morgan writes combined-format access logs there, so the exposed content includes request paths and parameters for every user -- tokens and identifiers included.
findings.missing_control: Restrict the mount to an authenticated support/admin role; logs are not public artefacts.
findings.falsifier: An authorisation middleware ahead of serveLogFiles(). The only adjacent call is verify.accessControlChallenges(), which records challenge state rather than enforcing access.

findings.title: Rate limiter keyed on an attacker-controlled header
findings.analysis: keyGenerator returns headers['X-Forwarded-For'] ?? ip. The header is client-supplied, so an attacker rotates it per request and each request lands in a fresh bucket -- the 100-per-5-minutes limit never binds, and the password-reset endpoint can be brute-forced.
findings.missing_control: Key on a trusted remote address derived from a validated proxy chain, not on a raw client header.
findings.falsifier: Proxy validation restricting which upstreams may set the header. app.enable('trust proxy') is set without a trusted-hop configuration, so the raw header wins.

findings.title: Product update endpoint left unauthorised
findings.analysis: Neighbouring product routes are guarded (POST requires isAuthorized, DELETE is denyAll) but the PUT line is commented out, so the auto-generated PUT /api/Products/:id inherits no authorisation at all. Any user can modify any product. The commented-out line is the tell: the control was written and then disabled, which is exactly the Phase 4 signature of a control being removed rather than never existing.
findings.missing_control: Re-enable an authorisation check on PUT /api/Products/:id, scoped to an admin role.
findings.falsifier: Authorisation applied to that verb elsewhere in the chain. The generated finale endpoint is reached with no such guard.

findings.title: Prometheus metrics endpoint served without authentication
findings.analysis: /metrics is registered with no authorisation middleware. The counters defined in routes/chat.ts alone (LLM token totals, per-tool call counts) leak internal usage and tool inventory; the standard process metrics add deployment detail useful for targeting.
findings.missing_control: Bind metrics to an internal interface or require an operator credential.
findings.falsifier: Any guard on the route registration. It is registered bare.

findings.title: Mass assignment on registration permits creating an admin account
findings.location: server.ts - generated /api/Users endpoints; models/user.ts role attribute
findings.analysis: User creation is served by an auto-generated finale endpoint over the whole model. The role attribute validates membership in ['customer','deluxe','accounting','admin'] but nothing strips it from client input, so a registration body carrying role: 'admin' is accepted and validates. The model's own setter treats an admin role as routine, swapping in an admin avatar. Marked Medium confidence because the generated router's field handling is not visible in the audited files -- the falsifier below is what would settle it.
findings.missing_control: An explicit write allow-list on registration (email, password only), with role assigned server-side.
findings.falsifier: A field allow-list or role-stripping middleware on POST /api/Users. The registered handlers are verify.registerAdminChallenge(), verify.passwordRepeatChallenge(), and verify.emptyUserRegistration() -- challenge-detection and input-shape checks, none of which restricts role.

findings.title: Product descriptions rendered through bypassSecurityTrustHtml
findings.analysis: Every product description is passed through DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml before rendering, explicitly disabling Angular's contextual escaping. Product records are writable through the REST API, so stored markup in a description executes in the browser of every user who views the listing -- persistent XSS.
findings.missing_control: Render descriptions as text, or sanitise with sanitizeHtml rather than bypassing the sanitiser.
findings.falsifier: Server-side sanitisation of description on write. Product descriptions are not sanitised on the write path.

findings.title: Search term from the query string reflected into the DOM
findings.analysis: filterTable() reads this.route.snapshot.queryParams.q and carries it into the rendered result heading without contextual escaping, so a crafted ?q= payload executes in the victim's browser from a shared link -- reflected/DOM XSS, with the bonus variant differing only in payload.
findings.missing_control: Interpolate the term through Angular's default escaping; never hand raw query text to an HTML sink.
findings.falsifier: Escaping between queryParams.q and the DOM sink. The value flows through unescaped.

findings.title: Privileged and unreleased routes enumerable from the client route table, guarded only client-side
findings.analysis: The Angular route table ships to the browser, so every path in it is discoverable by reading the bundle -- including administration, score-board, token-sale, and web3-sandbox. administration carries AdminGuard and accounting carries AccountingGuard, but an Angular guard is client-side code and controls only which component renders; it is not an authorisation boundary. score-board carries no guard at all. Anything these views reach must be independently authorised server-side.
findings.missing_control: Server-side authorisation on every API the privileged views consume; client-side guards are UX, not security.
findings.falsifier: Server-side role enforcement on the corresponding APIs would make the route disclosure cosmetic. That enforcement is the very thing JS6-15 and JS6-17 show to be incomplete.

findings.title: Account recovery rests on knowledge-based questions with publicly discoverable answers
findings.analysis: The password-reset flow authenticates on a single security question drawn from this file. Every option is low-entropy and externally researchable -- eldest sibling's middle name, mother's maiden name, favourite pet's name, teenage ZIP code. For any user with a public profile these are lookups, not secrets, which is why the documented reset challenges exist per-account rather than as one generic flaw. Combined with JS6-14 (a reset rate limiter that does not bind) the answers can also simply be guessed.
findings.missing_control: Replace single-factor KBA with an emailed, expiring, single-use token, and revoke sessions on reset.
findings.falsifier: A second factor or an emailed token requirement on the reset path. The reset flow accepts the security answer alone.
